identity.plain_name: A springy wire wound into a spiral (like a small, stiff Slinky) that pushes back when you squash it, pulls back when you stretch it, or twists back when you turn its arms; the ordinary spring inside pens, clothes pegs, mousetraps and garage doors
identity.term: Helical coil spring: compression spring, extension (tension) spring and helical torsion spring
aliases: coil spring, helical spring (Wikipedia 'Coil spring' and 'Spring (device)')
compression spring, push spring; open-coil helical spring (Lee Spring)
extension spring, tension spring, pull spring; close-wound spring with hooks or loops (Wikipedia; Lee Spring)
torsion spring, helical torsion spring; double torsion spring (one left-hand and one right-hand coil joined in the middle) (Wikipedia 'Torsion spring'; Lee Spring)
shapes: conical spring, hourglass (concave) spring, barrel (convex) spring, volute spring (Lee Spring; Wikipedia)
arc spring, bow spring; garter spring (an arc spring bent into a full circle) (Wikipedia 'Spring (device)')
drawbar spring (an extension-style spring that is actually squashed by loops passing through its middle) (Lee Spring)
continuous-length extension spring (cut to length) (Lee Spring)
pen spring, ballpoint pen spring (Wikimedia Commons category 'Ballpen springs')
music wire spring, piano wire spring (named after the usual spring steel wire)
Schraubenfeder (German, from the German Wikipedia link on 'Coil spring')
identity.one_liner: A length of springy wire wound into a helix that stores energy when it is squashed (compression spring), stretched (extension spring) or twisted by its arms (torsion spring), and gives it back as a push, a pull or a turning force roughly in proportion to how far it was moved.
identity.complexity: Single piece: one wound wire. A compression spring has plain, ground or closed ends that sit flat; an extension spring has close-wound coils with a hook or loop at each end; a torsion spring has a close-wound body with two straight or bent arms (legs). In use it needs the parts it works against: a seat, pocket, guide rod or hole for a compression spring, two anchor points (posts, holes or pins) for an extension spring, and a supporting rod (mandrel) plus two stops or slots for the legs of a torsion spring.
identity.how_it_works: Squashing or stretching a coil spring does not bend the wire much; it twists the wire along its length, so the steel acts like a long torsion bar wound into a small space, and the force rises steadily with the movement (Hooke's law) (Wikipedia 'Coil spring'). A torsion spring works the other way round: turning its arms bends the wire, winding the coils tighter so the coil diameter shrinks and the body gets longer (Wikipedia 'Torsion spring'; Lee Spring). An extension spring is wound with its coils pressed together (initial tension), so it does not stretch at all until you pull harder than that built-in force (RoyMech; MW Components). How stiff a spring is depends mostly on the wire thickness, the coil diameter and the number of working coils: thicker wire makes it much stiffer, while a wider coil or more coils make it softer (Engineers Edge).

job: store energy: pushes back (compression), pulls back (extension) or twists back (torsion) and returns parts to a rest position, e.g. the return spring in a button, latch, lever or hinge
tighten and hold tension: an extension or compression spring keeps a belt, cable, lid or clamp pressed or pulled with a steady force and takes up slack or wear
finder_attributes.motion: flex: a compression spring shortens along its axis until the coils touch (solid height); an extension spring lengthens along its axis; a torsion spring's arms rotate about the coil axis through part of a turn (stock torsion springs are sold with the arms at free angles from 90° to 360° apart, Lee Spring)
finder_attributes.degrees_of_freedom: 1 in intended use: along the axis for compression and extension springs, rotation about the axis for torsion springs. An unguided compression spring can also bend sideways (buckle) and an extension spring can swing on its hooks, which is why compression springs are often put over a rod or in a hole (Lee Spring)
special_behaviour: tensioning (takes up slack and holds): an extension or compression spring keeps a belt, cable, latch or lid under a steady force as parts move or wear

none of the other listed behaviours by itself: a coil spring is the 'engine' inside many clever mechanisms (click pens, ratchet pawls, detents, over-centre toggles, torque limiters, spring-applied brakes) but on its own it only pushes, pulls or twists back
extension springs have a built-in threshold (initial tension): nothing moves until the pull exceeds it, which helps hold things firmly shut (RoyMech; MW Components)
finder_attributes.holding_principle: spring force (it presses, pulls or twists the parts it sits between; it does not hold anything by itself unless something else, such as a latch or pawl, uses its force)
finder_attributes.removability: removable: a compression spring drops into a pocket or over a rod; an extension spring hooks onto posts or holes; a torsion spring slides over a rod with its legs in slots. It is usually trapped by the parts around it
finder_attributes.reuse_cycles: effectively unlimited, as long as it is not over-stressed: a correctly sized steel spring does not wear out from being fitted and removed. Its working life is limited by fatigue from loading cycles, e.g. Century Spring's stock extension springs list a suggested maximum stretch for an average life of around 50,000 cycles (MW Components), and garage door torsion springs are typically rated for 10,000-30,000 open-and-close cycles (Wikipedia 'Garage door')
finder_attributes.tools_needed: usually none; long-nose or looping pliers to stretch an extension spring onto its hooks (Lee Spring notes looping pliers for forming ends on cut-to-length springs), a spring hook or puller for strong extension springs, and a vice or clamp to squash a strong compression spring during assembly. Wire cutters or a cutting disc, a mandrel and a winding jig if you wind your own springs
finder_attributes.load: Light to heavy, depending on size: from tiny pen springs to car suspension and garage door springs that balance a door of 400 lb (about 180 kg) or more (Wikipedia 'Garage door'). Each type works in one direction only: compression springs take a push along the axis, extension springs a pull along the axis, torsion springs a twist that winds the coils tighter. They are weak sideways: a long compression spring buckles, extension spring hooks bend and break first, and a torsion spring loaded the wrong way (unwinding) is over-stressed (Lee Spring; MW Components)
finder_attributes.adjustable: Yes, by the way it is fitted: pre-compress a compression spring with a screw, nut or shims; move an extension spring's anchor point or add a tensioning screw; set a torsion spring's starting angle (preload). On the spring itself only by cutting coils off a compression spring (makes it stiffer and shorter) or cutting a continuous-length extension spring to size (Lee Spring). The rate (stiffness) of a given spring is fixed
finder_attributes.play_and_precision: not applicable as a locating part: it does not locate anything precisely, it only applies force. Force is predictable only between its free length and solid height; stock spring rates are typically held to about ±10% and extension spring initial tension is only a reference value (MW Components). Compression springs grow in diameter as they are squashed and torsion springs shrink in diameter and grow in length as they wind up, so both need clearance (Lee Spring). Standard squareness of a compression spring's ends is 3° (Lee Spring white paper)
finder_attributes.access_needed: not applicable: it sits between the parts it acts on and is fitted as they are assembled (a compression spring usually goes over the end of a rod or into a blind hole)
finder_attributes.materials: Usually spring steel wire: music wire (ASTM A228, high-carbon, the most common for small springs), oil-tempered and hard-drawn carbon steel, chrome-silicon and chrome-vanadium alloy steels for shock loads, stainless steel 302/304, 316 (marine) and 17-7 for corrosion and heat, and phosphor bronze or beryllium copper where the spring must carry electric current or be non-magnetic (Lee Spring 'Spring Material Options'; Wikipedia 'Spring (device)'). Plastic coil springs can be 3D printed from PETG or similar, but PLA makes a very poor spring (Hackaday, 2026) and all plastics lose force over time. Steel springs work against any material, but press on soft materials (plastic, wood) through a flat seat or washer so they do not dig in.
finder_attributes.maker_difficulty: easy: stock steel springs and assortment kits are cheap and easy to fit into printed or wooden parts. Moderate: winding your own from music wire on a printed jig works for small springs (Spring Factory, torsion spring winders). Printing a plastic coil spring is easy, but it will be weak and will creep

processes: off-the-shelf part: the usual choice (stock compression, extension and torsion springs, assortment kits, cut-to-length extension spring)
3D print (FDM): the housings, pockets, guide pins, posts and leg slots that hold a bought spring; plastic coil springs for light, occasional use (PETG, not PLA)
hand-wound from spring wire on a mandrel or printed winding jig (e.g. Spring Factory, torsion spring winders)
woodwork, laser cut and CNC: spring seats, anchor holes and pivot posts in wood, acrylic or metal parts
making.print_in_place: partly: a printed part can be designed around a pocket that a bought steel spring drops into (or is inserted during a pause), but the steel spring itself is never printed; plastic coil springs print as one piece (e.g. PETG coil springs on Printables) but are weak and creep, so they are not a substitute for steel
making.making_tips_3d_printing: Buy the spring and print the parts around it: plastic 'always permanently deforms under tension' over time and PLA makes a very poor spring material, while a steel spring costs pennies (Hackaday, 2026, article and comments). Design rules for the printed parts: (1) Compression springs: put the spring in a hole or over a guide pin; make the hole larger than the spring's outside diameter plus its tolerance and the growth in diameter as it is squashed, and the pin smaller than the inside diameter but not so small that it no longer stops buckling (Lee Spring). Always use a guide if the free length is more than about 4 times the mean coil diameter (Compression Spring Store). Add a hard stop so the spring never reaches solid height (all coils touching) in use (Lee Spring white paper). Buy springs with closed or closed-and-ground ends for a flat, square seat; plain ends are not recommended for heavily loaded or precise jobs (RoyMech). (2) Extension springs: anchor the hooks on round posts or pins with smooth, rounded edges, and keep the pull in line with the spring's axis; the hook is where an over-stressed extension spring breaks first (MW Components). FFF prints are stronger in one direction than another (Prusa), and a post printed standing up and pulled sideways loads the bonds between its layers [uncertain: the weak direction is inferred from Prusa's general statement], so use a steel pin or screw as the anchor for strong springs. (3) Torsion springs: support the coil on a rod about 90% of the spring's inside diameter at full wind-up, not much smaller (Lee Spring), give the legs slots or stops, load it so it winds tighter, and leave room for the body to get longer as it winds (Lee Spring). A steel pin or screw makes a better arbor than a thin printed peg. (4) If you must print a coil spring: PETG with 100% infill worked for a 20 cm PETG coil spring on Printables; printing the spring with support along its whole length helped one designer print PETG springs consistently (Printables 'Parametric Supported Spring', 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.15 mm layers, 3 perimeters); a special g-code method can print springs in mid-air, but they are 'functional, albeit not very strong' (Hackaday, 2018). Plastic springs are best where they rest unloaded and are only occasionally compressed (Hackaday 2026 comment). (5) To make your own steel springs, print a winding jig: the Spring Factory uses a threaded mandrel for even coil spacing and takes piano wire of about 0.8-1.2 mm (Hackaday, 2022); torsion-spring winders use a drill-bit shank as the mandrel. Springs spring open after winding, so the finished coil is larger than the mandrel (Printables 'Extension spring jig' and 'Torsion Spring Winding Jig', which points to a spring mandrel calculator).
making.off_the_shelf_parts: Stock compression springs (music wire, stainless steel 302/304, chrome silicon; plain, ground, closed or closed-and-ground ends; conical, hourglass and barrel shapes); stock extension springs with machine hooks, crossover-centre loops, full loops, extended or reduced eyes and threaded-insert ends; continuous-length extension spring (cut to length and form your own loops); drawbar springs; stock torsion springs with straight legs at 90°, 120°, 180°, 210°, 270°, 300° or 360° free leg angles, left-hand or right-hand wind, and double torsion springs; micro springs for small devices (all from Lee Spring's catalogue pages); spring assortment kits (compression, extension and torsion; Lee Spring 'Spring Kits', generic mixed kits); spring wire (music wire ASTM A228, stainless 302/304, 316, 17-7 PH) for winding your own; guide rods, shoulder bolts and dowel pins as spring guides and anchors.
rules_of_thumb: Spring rate (stiffness) of a compression or extension spring: k = G d^4 / (8 n D^3), with G the shear modulus of the wire, d the wire diameter, n the number of active coils and D the mean coil diameter (outside diameter minus wire diameter) (Engineers Edge, https://www.engineersedge.com/spring_comp_calc_k.htm). So doubling the wire thickness makes the spring 16 times stiffer, while doubling the coil diameter makes it 8 times softer. Worked example (own calculation, using G = 11.5 x 10^6 psi, about 79 GPa, for music wire from Lee Spring, https://www.leespring.com/spring-materials): 1 mm wire, 9 mm mean diameter, 10 active coils gives about 1.4 N per mm.

Keep the spring index C (mean coil diameter / wire diameter) between about 3 and 12 for most helical springs (RoyMech, https://roymech.org/Useful_Tables/Springs/Springs_helical.html); very tight coils are hard to wind and highly stressed, and very open ones are floppy. The Lee Spring white paper also says to check the index and that the pitch must not exceed the outside diameter (https://www.leespring.com/sites/default/files/pdf/Lee%20Spring%20-%20WhitePaper%20-%20Spring%20Design%20General%20Consideration_US.pdf).

A compression spring whose free length is more than about 4 times its mean coil diameter is likely to buckle; fix it with a larger diameter, shorter length, more coils, or by running it over a rod or in a hole (Compression Spring Store, https://www.compressionspring.com/slenderness-ratio-making-your-spring-buckle.html).

Make a guide hole larger than the spring's outside diameter, allowing for tolerance and for the diameter growing as it is compressed; make a guide rod smaller than the inside diameter but not so small that it stops preventing buckling (Lee Spring, https://www.leespring.com/learn-about-compression-springs and white paper https://www.leespring.com/sites/default/files/pdf/Lee%20Spring%20-%20WhitePaper%20-%20Spring%20Design%20General%20Consideration_US.pdf).

Every working height must be above solid height (all coils touching); allow 5% on the nominal solid height. Total coils = active coils for open ends, +1 for open-and-ground ends, +2 for closed or closed-and-ground ends (Lee Spring white paper, https://www.leespring.com/sites/default/files/pdf/Lee%20Spring%20-%20WhitePaper%20-%20Spring%20Design%20General%20Consideration_US.pdf; RoyMech end-design table).

Stress: for general-purpose springs a maximum of about 40% of the wire's tensile strength may be used (RoyMech). If the stress at a working height is above 40% of tensile strength the spring will take a permanent set unless it is pre-set; above 60% it must be redesigned (Lee Spring white paper).

Torsion springs: always load them in the direction that makes the coil diameter smaller (winds them tighter); the residual stresses from forming help in that direction and hurt in the other. Support them on a rod about 90% of the inside diameter at full deflection, not much smaller, and allow for the body getting longer as it winds up. Specify the direction of wind (Lee Spring, https://www.leespring.com/learn-about-torsion-springs). If the loaded inside diameter shrinks onto the shaft, the spring will fail (RoyMech, https://roymech.org/Useful_Tables/Springs/Springs_Torsion.html).

Extension springs: the force at any stretch = initial tension + rate x stretch; the initial tension must be overcome before the spring starts to stretch. Stresses are highest where the last coil turns into the hook, so an over-stressed extension spring fails at the hook first; the suggested body stress is 30-45% of the wire's minimum tensile strength (MW Components / Century Spring, https://www.mwcomponents.com/how-to-select-an-extension-spring).

Springs in parallel add their stiffnesses; springs in series add their softness (compliance), so two identical springs end to end are half as stiff (Wikipedia 'Spring (device)', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_(device)).

Maximum operating temperatures for common spring wires: music wire and carbon steels about 250 °F (121 °C); oil-tempered chrome silicon 475 °F (246 °C); stainless 302/304 and 316 about 550 °F (288 °C); 17-7 PH stainless 650 °F (343 °C); phosphor bronze 200 °F (93 °C) (Lee Spring, https://www.leespring.com/spring-materials).

Extension springs that balance heavy things (e.g. garage doors) should always have a safety cable running through the middle, tied to solid points at both ends, so a broken spring cannot fly (Wikipedia 'Garage door', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garage_door).

Repelling magnets as a spring (magnetic spring): the force 'doesn't increase in a straight line like the spring'; it stays very weak for most of the travel and then rises very quickly. In K&J's scale pogo-stick test two repelling ring magnets stored less than 0.32 J (2.8 in-lb) when fully compressed, against about 1.65 J (14.6 in-lb) for the coil spring; adding more magnets raised the force but the stack's thickness cut the travel (K&J Magnetics, https://www.kjmagnetics.com/blog/magnetic-springs).

everyday_examples: the compression spring inside a click ballpoint pen (Wikimedia Commons has a whole category of 'Ballpen springs')
the torsion spring in a wooden clothes peg and in a classic snap mousetrap (Wikipedia 'Torsion spring')
the extension springs around the edge of a trampoline and on the side of an up-and-over garage door (Lee Spring; Wikipedia 'Garage door')
the coiled battery contact spring in a TV remote or torch (Wikipedia 'Spring (device)')
guidance.when_to_use: Whenever something needs to spring back by itself: return buttons, triggers, levers, latches and lids to their rest position; keep a belt, cable or clamp under steady tension; press a detent ball, pawl or friction pad into place; balance a hinged part; or cushion a bump. Choose a compression spring for a push (it is also safest, because when it breaks the pieces are still trapped between the parts), an extension spring for a pull between two points (it needs no guide and its initial tension holds things firmly shut), and a torsion spring to turn something back about a hinge pin, such as a spring-loaded lid, door or clip. For a maker, a bought steel spring is almost always better than a printed or improvised one.
guidance.when_not_to_use: Not where there is very little height: use wave springs or disc (Belleville) springs, which give the same force in much less space. Not for long travel with nearly constant force: use a constant-force spring or a gas spring. Not for long-lasting force made from printed plastic: plastic creeps and relaxes, so use a steel spring or at least PETG and accept a short life; for a printed one-piece spring a flat leaf spring or ortho-planar spring prints better than a coil. Not for twisting a torsion spring the 'opening' way: turn it round or use a spring wound the other hand. Not as a shock absorber on its own: a spring stores and returns energy and will bounce, so add a damper. Not for precise positioning: a spring only gives force, so use a stop, detent or locating feature to set the position. Not where the push has to work across a gap or through a wall with no contact: repelling magnets can act as a spring (a magnetic spring) and work across an air gap, though they cost more than coil springs and their force stays weak until they are close together, then rises very steeply (K&J Magnetics 'Magnetic springs'); see Magnetic detent.
guidance.environment_limits: Heat: music wire and carbon-steel springs are rated to about 121 °C (250 °F), stainless 302/304 and 316 to about 288 °C, 17-7 PH stainless to about 343 °C and phosphor bronze to about 93 °C (Lee Spring); above these they take a set and lose force. Water and corrosion: bare music wire rusts (it is sold uncoated, or zinc or cadmium plated; Lee Spring), so use stainless steel outdoors and 316 in salt water (Lee Spring notes it resists chloride attack); humid coastal air noticeably shortens garage door spring life (Wikipedia 'Garage door'). Fatigue: springs that cycle a lot must be stressed less; stock extension spring maximum loads are set for about 50,000 cycles (MW Components). Over-stress: a spring squashed or stretched too far takes a permanent set (gets shorter or longer) and loses force (Lee Spring). Printed plastic springs creep under steady load and lose most of their springiness over months (Hackaday, 2026, reader comments), and soften at much lower temperatures than steel.
guidance.safety_notes: Stored energy: large springs, especially garage door torsion springs, are extremely dangerous; many people have been injured or killed adjusting them, and a broken spring or failed part can fly off or let a heavy door fall (Wikipedia 'Garage door'); leave these to trained people. Extension springs on doors and heavy balances need a safety cable through the middle (Wikipedia). Winding or cutting spring wire: the wire whips or stabs when tension is released and cut ends are sharp; wear eye protection and cut-resistant gloves (warnings on the Printables 'Extension spring jig' and 'Metal Torsion Spring Maker' pages). Small compression springs can shoot out when a part is taken apart; point it away from your face. Pinch points between coils of extension springs and between a torsion spring's legs.
guidance.common_failures: (1) Buckling: a long, thin compression spring bows sideways and can pop out; guide it on a rod or in a hole, or use a shorter, fatter spring (Compression Spring Store; Lee Spring). (2) Binding: the spring rubs or jams because its diameter grows (compression) or shrinks (torsion) under load; leave clearance (Lee Spring; RoyMech). (3) Bottoming out (going solid) and taking a set: squashed until all coils touch, it gets permanently shorter and weaker; add a hard stop or pick a spring with more travel (Lee Spring white paper). (4) Broken hooks on extension springs: the hook is the most stressed point; keep the pull in line and choose a spring with a lower stress or a better end (MW Components). (5) Torsion spring loaded the wrong way (unwinding), or a mandrel that is too big: over-stress and early breakage; check the direction of wind and size the rod to about 90% of the loaded inside diameter (Lee Spring). (6) Fatigue cracks after many cycles, and corrosion; use stainless or coated springs and keep stresses low. (7) Plastic springs slowly losing their push (creep); replace with steel.
related: Wave and disc springs (compact axial springs): give the same push as a coil spring in much less height, but with shorter travel
Constant-force spring (spring-return reel): a rolled steel strip that pulls with almost the same force over a long distance, unlike a coil spring whose force rises as it stretches

Spiral power spring (clock spring): a flat strip wound in a flat spiral that gives a fairly steady turning force over large angles or several whole turns (Wikipedia 'Torsion spring'); a helical torsion spring is for smaller angles
Gas spring: a sealed cylinder of compressed gas that pushes over long travel with nearly steady force and some built-in damping
Printed leaf spring (flat cantilever spring) and ortho-planar spring: springs that are easy to 3D print or laser cut in one piece, instead of a wound wire
Ball detent (spring plunger) and self-closing (spring) hinges: ready-made parts that use a coil spring inside for clicking or closing
Wrap-spring clutch: uses a close-wound coil spring gripping a shaft as a one-way clutch rather than as an energy store
Spring balancer (gravity compensation): arranges coil springs so they cancel the weight of an arm or lid at every angle
Shock-corded sectional pole and elastic cord: rubber is a softer, cheaper tension spring that also damps, but it ages and creeps faster than steel

Magnetic detent: magnet click stops; repelling magnets can also be used as a spring (magnetic spring), which works across an air gap but whose force rises steeply only at the end of travel (K&J Magnetics)
Battery holder and battery contacts: a coil (often conical) spring presses on one end of a cell as its contact
Pogo pin: a spring-loaded contact pin, where a tiny compression spring inside a tube pushes a contact pin out against a pad
